research_participation.name: Adaptive and plastic potential of ectotherm physiology for responding to climate change
research_participation.summary: Whether traits involved in metabolism and water retention allow lizards living along climatic gradients to respond to climate change through adaptation or plasticity.
description: Can lizards keep up with a warming, drying climate? WETADAPT asked how much of their physiology, especially metabolism and the ability to hold on to water, can adapt or adjust.

The project compared populations of two mountain lizards sampled along long elevation gradients: *Gallotia galloti* in the subtropical climate of Tenerife and *Iberolacerta horvathi* in temperate Slovenia. Work packages linked physiology to present-day climate, looked for genes under selection and changes in gene expression, and fed the results into mechanistic models that forecast how the species may respond to future climates.

research_participation.name: Slovenia's Strategic Integrated LIFE Project for Adaptation
research_participation.summary: Implements Slovenia's national strategy for adaptation to climate change, with pilot measures in agriculture, forestry, nature conservation, health, water management and the economy.
description: One of Slovenia's largest climate-adaptation projects: 14 partners and 5 associated organisations, led by the national environment ministry, working until 2032 to make the country more resilient to heat waves, droughts, floods and fires.

The project implements Slovenia's Strategic Framework for Climate Change Adaptation through 14 pilot measures in water management, agriculture, forestry, nature conservation, public health and the economy, and sets up a national centre for climate analyses and projections. I lead and coordinate the National Institute of Biology's part of the work.

research_participation.name: Evolutionary effects of competition in coexisting apex predator populations
research_participation.summary: Competition between coexisting owl species and its evolutionary effects.
description: What does competition do to two predators that share the same forest over many generations? CO-STRIX studies the ecological and evolutionary effects of competition between coexisting apex predators.

It builds on Al Vrezec's long-term work on two forest owls, the tawny owl, *Strix aluco*, and the Ural owl, *Strix uralensis*, a natural pair for testing how competition shapes where predators live, what they eat and how their populations respond to the environment.

research_participation.name: Revealing ecological roles of apex predators in extreme environments
research_participation.summary: The ecological roles of apex predators, such as the lynx in high mountains, in extreme environments.
description: Apex predators feed more than themselves. ExtremePredator studies how the prey they leave behind moves nutrients through ecosystems where life is hardest: high mountains under long snow cover and deserts with almost no rain.

Camera traps follow which scavengers feed on kills of Eurasian lynx, cheetahs and brown hyenas, and GPS tags track golden eagles. Stable isotopes trace nitrogen carried from sea to land through soil, plants, insects and lizards, and show how hyenas change plant growth in the desert.

research_participation.name: Communities, interactions and communications in ecosystems
description: The National Institute of Biology's long-term research programme on how organisms interact and communicate, from individuals to whole ecosystems. My project work sits within it.

hero_quote.text: Though natural history studies may be difficult and arduous, for many of us they are fun to do: one works with live animals in natural environments, students can usefully participate, ingenious experiments must be designed, visits to interesting places are involved, and, when modern laboratory analyses are required, one can often find somebody else to do the lab work.
hero_quote.author: A. Stanley Rand
